headline: High-risk shared filesystem and shell access create prompt-injection, data-leakage, and cascading-error exposure between CrewAI and ms-swift.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: CrewAI reads and writes the host working directory and can ingest tool/file content as crew inputs; ms-swift also reads and writes files and runs CLI/Python workflows. With no isolation or provenance controls stated, content from one can be treated as instructions by the other through shared files. The interaction is plausible in default setups, though not directly documented.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same working directory, file content from one can influence the other.
IF either agent parses shared files or logs as instructions, prompt injection becomes feasible.
mitigations: Use separate directories for each agent.
Disable automatic parsing of shared files as instructions.
Add a provenance tag to every inter-agent artifact.
Run each agent in a separate container with read-only mounts where possible.
requires-engineering: add an allowlist for trusted inter-agent message formats.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents can read and write filesystem content, and CrewAI explicitly handles developer-passed crew data plus API keys, while ms-swift touches datasets, checkpoints, logs, and hub/sdk tokens. If they share a workspace, sensitive artifacts can flow from one agent into the other's outputs or uploads. The profiles do not show hard isolation, so the leakage path is credible.
conditions: IF the agents share a workspace or mounted volume, files can be exposed across both.
IF either agent uploads local files to external model or hub APIs, sensitive data can leave the host.
mitigations: Separate secrets from shared work directories.
Mount only the minimum required files into each agent.
Rotate any exposed API or hub tokens.
Review logs for accidental secret capture.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem ACLs and secret redaction.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write and subprocess execution, and CrewAI supports multiple instances with developer-defined shared state while ms-swift does not state locking or coordination. If they operate on the same directory or mutable artifacts, concurrent writes can corrupt files, checkpoints, or configs. Uncertainty about locking pushes this to high because the blast radius can be irreversible.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, file corruption or overwrite races can occur.
IF either agent mutates shared checkpoints or configs without locks, state can become unrecoverable.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories.
Serialize writes with a simple lock file.
Back up mutable artifacts before concurrent runs.
Avoid concurrent checkpoint edits.
requires-engineering: add transactional writes or orchestration-level locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: CrewAI is a multi-agent orchestration framework that can pass outputs between agents, and ms-swift is a CLI/Python stack that can consume configs, datasets, and evaluation outputs. If CrewAI-generated content is treated as authoritative by ms-swift, errors can cascade into downstream training, evaluation, or support actions. The profiles suggest the pathway but do not prove default trust, so medium fits.
conditions: IF CrewAI output is fed into ms-swift configs, datasets, or checkpoints without review, errors propagate.
IF ms-swift acts on generated artifacts automatically, a bad upstream result can cascade.
mitigations: Insert a human review step before handoff.
Validate schemas for all inter-agent artifacts.
Keep generated outputs separate from source datasets.
Log provenance for each artifact.
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks before downstream execution.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and do not state conflicting residency, certification, or retention regimes. CrewAI handles developer-passed crew data and ms-swift handles datasets, checkpoints, and logs, but no explicit compliance mismatch is documented. The main issue is incomplete documentation rather than a proven violation, so low is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is introduced into either agent, compliance review becomes necessary.
IF the deployment imposes residency or retention rules not reflected in the profiles, a mismatch may emerge.
mitigations: Confirm data classification before use.
Keep regulated data out of both agents unless approved.
Document retention and deletion settings.
Review vendor and hosting region settings.
requires-engineering: implement policy enforcement for residency and retention.
